Day 67 of 100 · Docker

Docker Compose

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityDockerPublished artifact recovered

Docker Compose describes a multi-container application, its network, storage, environment and startup relationships in one version-controlled file.

Architecture / mental model

compose.yaml → db + app + network + volume + health relationship

How it works

The published stack defined PostgreSQL and an application together, attached persistent `db-data`, supplied application connection data and mapped the application to a host port.

A database health check used `pg_isready`, and the application dependency used `condition: service_healthy` rather than assuming process start meant service readiness.

Compose reduces command-memory debt. The point is not merely fewer terminal lines; the system topology becomes inspectable in one declarative artifact.

Hands-on reference

docker compose config
docker compose up -d
docker compose ps
docker compose logs -f
docker compose down

Verification

Run `docker compose config` to inspect the resolved configuration, start the stack, confirm database health and make a real application request. Restart or recreate services and verify storage/network behavior remains correct.

Field note / gotcha

`depends_on` startup ordering does not by itself mean the dependency is ready to serve requests. Health-aware conditions are needed when application startup truly depends on readiness.

Security considerations

Keep real credentials outside committed Compose files, limit host port bindings and avoid mounting the Docker socket into services unless the threat model explicitly accepts host-level control.

What I learned

A multi-container application becomes easier to reproduce when topology is code instead of shell history.
